evidence.claim: Gulf Coast cities and architecture along the Tampa-to-Miami road
evidence.quote: The highway takes travelers through the many wonderful Florida cities such as Palmetto, Bradenton, Sarasota, Venice, and North Port, all rich with culture, architecture, recreation, and history.

evidence.claim: Gulf Coast cities and architecture along the Tampa-to-Miami road
evidence.quote: from State Road 60 (SR 60) in Tampa to US 1 in Miami.

evidence.claim: The Windows to the Gulf Coast Waters Scenic Highway follows 70 miles of US 41 through Florida’s Gulf Coast cities.
evidence.quote: The Tamiami Trail – Windows to the Gulf Coast Waters Scenic Highway flows along US 41 from the Sarasota/Charlotte County line to the Manatee/Hillsborough County line for 70 miles.

evidence.claim: Designated in December 2003, the byway combines recreation with urban stops for walking and sightseeing, as Florida Scenic Highways emphasizes.
evidence.quote: Recreational opportunities, as well as urban experiences such as shopping, walking, and sightseeing, are found all along the highway.

evidence.claim: Designated in December 2003, the byway combines recreation with urban stops for walking and sightseeing, as Florida Scenic Highways emphasizes.
evidence.quote: Designated: December 19, 2003

evidence.claim: In Sarasota, the trail briefly follows Bayfront Drive before turning north parallel to the coast.
evidence.quote: after briefly following Bayfront Drive, the Trail heads north again paralleling the coast

evidence.claim: This corridor belongs to the longer Tamiami Trail linking Tampa and Miami.
evidence.quote: The Tamiami Trail () is the southernmost 284 miles (457 km) of U.S. Highway 41 (US 41) from State Road 60 (SR 60) in Tampa to US 1 in Miami.

evidence.claim: In 1915, Francis W. Perry of the Fort Myers Chamber of Commerce and Miami’s James F. Jaudon began campaigning for a cross-peninsula highway.
evidence.quote: The idea for a trans-peninsula highway that connected the west and east coasts of Florida originated in April 1915 at an informal meeting in Tallahassee between Francis W. Perry, then president of the Fort Myers Chamber of Commerce, and James F. Jaudon of Miami

evidence.claim: In 1915, Francis W. Perry of the Fort Myers Chamber of Commerce and Miami’s James F. Jaudon began campaigning for a cross-peninsula highway.
evidence.quote: after which they returned to their respective cities and began advocating for the construction of what was originally called the Miami to Marco Highway.

evidence.claim: When state construction funds for the east-west section ran out in 1922, Barron Collier pledged the following year to finance its completion.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the State of Florida ran out of construction funds for the east–west portion. The following year, Barron Collier, an advertising mogul who had recently diversified his holdings by investing in various types of businesses and millions of acres of southwest Florida wilderness, pledged that he would bankroll the completion of the Tamiami Trail;

evidence.claim: The full trail opened on April 26, 1928.
evidence.quote: The Tamiami Trail officially opened on April 26, 1928.

evidence.claim: The northern alignment changed in 1951: between Tampa and Palmetto, US 41 shifted from the inland route through Riverview and Parrish to the route through Ruskin and Apollo Beach.
evidence.quote: The original alignment ran further inland through Riverview and Parrish.  The route was realigned to its current route through Ruskin and Apollo Beach in 1951

evidence.claim: The northern alignment changed in 1951: between Tampa and Palmetto, US 41 shifted from the inland route through Riverview and Parrish to the route through Ruskin and Apollo Beach.
evidence.quote: The alignment of the Tamiami Trail and US 41 at the north end between Tampa and Palmetto was also changed in the 1950s.

evidence.claim: At Venice, the numbered highway and the older trail alignment diverge: US 41 was rerouted onto a bypass in 1965, while Business US 41 marks the former alignment.
evidence.quote: In 1965, US 41 was rerouted as a bypass along unsigned SR 45A around Venice Gardens, while Business US 41 signs mark the three-mile-long (4.8 km) former alignment (which is still named Tamiami Trail).

evidence.claim: Drive this coastal byway south from the Manatee-Hillsborough county line through Palmetto and Bradenton, then Sarasota, Venice and North Port, ending at the Sarasota-Charlotte line.
evidence.quote: The highway takes travelers through the many wonderful Florida cities such as Palmetto, Bradenton, Sarasota, Venice, and North Port

evidence.claim: Drive this coastal byway south from the Manatee-Hillsborough county line through Palmetto and Bradenton, then Sarasota, Venice and North Port, ending at the Sarasota-Charlotte line.
evidence.quote: from the Sarasota/Charlotte County line to the Manatee/Hillsborough County line for 70 miles.

evidence.claim: John and Mable Ringling’s winter residence beside Sarasota Bay brought Venetian architecture to a Florida waterfront.
evidence.quote: Cà d'Zan () is a Mediterranean revival residence in Sarasota, Florida, adjacent to Sarasota Bay.

evidence.claim: John and Mable Ringling’s winter residence beside Sarasota Bay brought Venetian architecture to a Florida waterfront.
evidence.quote: Cà d'Zan was built in the mid-1920s as the winter retreat of the American circus mogul, entrepreneur, and art collector John Ringling and his wife Mable Burton Ringling.

evidence.claim: Their visits to Venice inspired its Gothic-arched windows and terra cotta ornament.
evidence.quote: Mable and John Ringling had visited Venice, which inspired the Venetian Gothic influence in the house, prominently seen in a variety of architectural elements such as windows with Gothic arches and terra cotta ornament replicating Gothic tracery.

evidence.claim: Architect Dwight James Baum designed the house; Owen Burns built it between 1924 and 1926.
evidence.quote: they commissioned the architect, Dwight James Baum, to design a new winter residence. Construction of the new residence by Owen Burns began in 1924 and was completed in 1926.

evidence.claim: Its 56 rooms included a ballroom and great hall for entertaining.
evidence.quote: With a total of fifty-six rooms, the Cà d'Zan was meant to impress as a showplace for entertaining. Its first floor consists mainly of principal rooms for entertaining, including a reception room, lounging room, breakfast room, dining room, great hall, and ballroom.

evidence.claim: The name means House of John in Venetian. After John Ringling’s death, the residence formed part of his bequest to the state of Florida.
evidence.quote: The name Cà d'Zan means "House of John" in the Venetian language

evidence.claim: The name means House of John in Venetian. After John Ringling’s death, the residence formed part of his bequest to the state of Florida.
evidence.quote: Cà d'Zan was part of John Ringling's bequest to the state of Florida

evidence.claim: The waterfront setting also brought damage: Hurricanes Helene and Milton flooded the basement and damaged the terrace in 2024.
evidence.quote: In September and October 2024, Ca' d'Zan took significant damage from Hurricanes Helene and Milton which hit within two weeks of each other. Eight feet of water flooded the basement

evidence.claim: The waterfront setting also brought damage: Hurricanes Helene and Milton flooded the basement and damaged the terrace in 2024.
evidence.quote: The waterfront terrace suffered significant damage from two boats crashing into the support structures.

evidence.claim: The mansion closed to visitors indefinitely after Hurricane Helene in September 2024.
evidence.quote: The mansion was closed to visitors indefinitely after Hurricane Helene in the last week of September 2024.

evidence.claim: Venice’s planned streets began with a surgeon’s land purchase during the 1920s Florida boom.
evidence.quote: During the Florida land boom of the 1920s, Fred H. Albee, an orthopedic surgeon renowned for his bone-grafting operations, bought 112 acres (45 ha) from Bertha Palmer to develop Venice.

evidence.claim: Venice’s planned streets began with a surgeon’s land purchase during the 1920s Florida boom.
evidence.quote: He hired John Nolen to plan the city and create a master plan for the streets.

evidence.claim: Fred H. Albee hired John Nolen to lay out the city, then sold the land to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, retaining Nolen as planner.
evidence.quote: He hired John Nolen to plan the city and create a master plan for the streets. Albee sold the land to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and retained Nolen as city planner.

evidence.claim: The first city infrastructure took shape in 1925 and 1926.
evidence.quote: The first portions of the city and infrastructure were constructed in 1925–1926.

evidence.claim: Earlier fishermen knew the place as Horse and Chaise, after a carriage-shaped formation of trees.
evidence.quote: Venice was first known as "Horse and Chaise" because of a carriage-like tree formation that marked the spot for fishermen.

evidence.claim: The Venice name first accompanied an 1888 post office, suggested by Frank Higel for the place’s resemblance to the Italian canal city.
evidence.quote: In 1888, another post office was established, this time with the name "Venice", a name Higel himself suggested because of its likeness to the canal city in Italy.

evidence.claim: What residents call Venice Island is mainland reached by bridges across the artificial Intracoastal Waterway.
evidence.quote: The city includes what locals call "Venice Island", a portion of the mainland that is accessed via bridges over the artificially created Intracoastal Waterway.

evidence.claim: A free-flowing artesian spring distinguishes Warm Mineral Springs, where a large part of the area has been annexed into North Port.
evidence.quote: The Warm Mineral Springs locale is notable for a free-flowing artesian spring. A large portion of the area was annexed by the municipality of North Port, and is now part of that city.

evidence.claim: The community also has a modernist architectural landmark: Victor Lundy designed the Warm Mineral Springs Motel.
evidence.quote: The Warm Mineral Springs Motel designed by modernist architect Victor Lundy

evidence.claim: Lundy was associated with the Sarasota School of Architecture, and the motel is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: one of the architects associated with the Sarasota School of Architecture, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

flags: Ca’ d’Zan cache reports indefinite closure after September 2024; no cached manager update or reopening confirmation. Retained the landmark, omitted a notice or invitation to enter, and dated the cache-only practical check as requested.
Warm Mineral Springs kept short: cache supplies the spring and landmark architect but no spring geology, site history or current visitor access.
Official 70-mile byway length differs from catalog mapped 59.4 miles; use the official corridor length.
North-to-south presentation follows ascending strip miles, reversing the current story’s direction.
Cache offers city sequence and Sarasota road character but no corridor-wide lane, grade or travel-time account.
Corrected Collier pledge to 1923 and identified the east-west funding gap; the official overview compresses the wider trail history into this corridor.
